items.title: Mystery guest-onderzoek: zo maken bibliotheken werk van klantinzichten
items.raw_text: Zeven bibliotheken namen in 2025 deel aan het mystery guest-onderzoek via Probiblio. Met de klantinzichten die dit opleverde zijn de bibliotheken aan de slag gegaan om de klantbeleving te verbeteren. Elke bibliotheek koos daarbij een eigen route. Na een half jaar wisselden de bibliotheken met elkaar uit welke stappen gezet zijn of nog op de agenda staan. Ter inspiratie delen we enkele succesvolle acties. Bij vrijwel alle deelnemende bibliotheken leiden de klantinzichten uit het mystery guest-onderzoek tot goede gesprekken waarom de klantervaringen soms afweken van verwachtingen en hoe hierop bijgestuurd kan worden. De uitkomsten van het onderzoek gaven zowel herkenning als soms ook verbazing, maar ook dat was aanleiding tot een goed gesprek. En soms ook reden om met de hele groep nog eens samen door de bibliotheek te lopen om te bekijken hoe het toch kan dat bezoekers iets anders zien en ervaren dan jij dacht dat ze ervaren. items.title: Caribische bibliotheken versterken samenwerking tijdens uitwisselingsweek in El Salvador
items.raw_text: Hoe bouw je samen aan een sterk netwerk van bibliotheken, terwijl je ook over grenzen heen van elkaar blijft leren? Die vraag stond centraal tijdens een bijzondere uitwisselingsweek in El Salvador. Bibliotheken uit het Caribisch deel van ons Koninkrijk kwamen samen om kennis en ervaringen met elkaar te delen en om een belangrijke stap te zetten in hun gezamenlijke ontwikkeling. Tijdens de conferentie ondertekenden Biblioteka Nashonal Kòrsou , Biblioteca Nacional Aruba , Biblioteka Públiko Boneiru , Sint Maarten Library , Gertrude Judson Bicentennial Public Library St. Eustatius en Queen Wilhelmina Library hun gezamenlijke netwerkplan. Daarmee bekrachtigen zij hun gedeelde ambities en afspraken voor de komende periode. Een netwerk met ambitie De Caribische bibliotheken werken, met begeleiding van Common Eye , aan een sterk en duurzaam netwerk dat aansluit bij hun eigen behoeften, ervaringen en ambities. Het netwerkplan richt zich onder andere op een sterkere positionering van de Caribische bibliotheken en de ontwikkeling van toekomstbestendige bibliotheken. Als kennis- en expertisepartner zijn wij vanuit Rijnbrink, samen met de Koninklijke Bibliotheek (KB) , betrokken bij het netwerk. We ondersteunen de bibliotheken bij hun organisatorische en inhoudelijke ontwikkeling en helpen mee om de ambities uit het netwerkplan verder te brengen. items.title: Hoe de VoorleesExpress gezinnen versterkt en bibliotheken scherper laat werken

items.title: Prentenboeken in Papiamentu: een feest van herkenning
items.raw_text: Een prentenboek vertalen lijkt eenvoudig: je zet de ene taal om in de andere. Maar hoe zorg je ervoor dat een kind zich écht herkent in een verhaal? Voor de nieuwe Papiamentu-prentenboeken – gerealiseerd in het project Leesbevordering in meertalige gezinnen – dachten leden van de klankbordgroep mee over taal, cultuur en geschiedenis. Waarom is de keuze voor opa beter dan de officiële vertaling tawela? Waarom mocht het verhaal van Tula in de nieuwe prentenboekencollectie niet ontbreken? En wat gebeurt er als een kind voor het eerst een verhaal in zijn eigen taal hoort? Jakeema, Myrthe en Margriet vertellen hoe juist die keuzes het verschil maken. Waarom vertalen nodig was Zoals het eerdere artikel over dit project al aangaf: voorlezen stimuleert de taalontwikkeling van jonge kinderen het beste. Juist voorlezen in de thuistaal, de taal van het hart, levert veel extra’s op. Ouders op Bonaire willen dat met alle liefde doen, vertelt Jakeema Hernandez, programmaleider bij Bibliotheek Bonaire. Maar de collectie prentenboeken in het Papiamentu is beperkt. Jakeema is dan ook blij met de nieuwe, vertaalde Papiamentu-boeken. Als kind hield ik al van lezen, maar een boek in mijn eigen taal vinden in de boekhandel of bibliotheek was onmogelijk. Voor mijn inner child is het mooi om te zien dat er nu boeken in het Papiamentu bestaan. items.title: Privacy & informatiebeveiliging: dit speelt er in de bibliotheek
items.raw_text: Privacy en informatiebeveiliging zijn belangrijke onderwerpen voor iedere bibliotheek. Maar wat betekenen nieuwe ontwikkelingen nu concreet voor de praktijk? items.title: Voorlezen in de taal van je hart: meer verhalen in Farsi en Papiamentu
items.raw_text: Een Curaçaos meisje dat glundert als ze het boek ‘Mihó nò’ ontdekt tussen de bibliotheekboeken. Of een Farsi-sprekende moeder die ontroerd raakt, als ze tijdens een bijeenkomst hoort dat dromen en schelden in je thuistaal normaal is. items.title: Haal meer uit data voor maatschappelijke programmering met de Datateam®methode
items.raw_text: Hoe maak je keuzes rond programmering die niet alleen goed voelen, maar ook goed onderbouwd zijn? Die vraag stond centraal tijdens de inspirerende en energieke workshop Haal meer uit data – De Datateam®methode op 4 juni bij Kunstwerk! in Zevenaar. Van vraagstuk naar inzicht Tijdens de interactieve workshop wisselden theorie en praktijk elkaar af. Deelnemers gingen aan de slag met vraagstukken uit hun eigen organisatie. items.title: HR Actueel – Mogelijke afschaffing compensatie transitievergoeding: wat betekent dit voor bibliotheken?
items.raw_text: Vanaf 2027 ontvangen werkgevers mogelijk geen compensatie meer voor de transitievergoeding bij ontslag wegens langdurige arbeidsongeschiktheid. Dat heeft het kabinet aangekondigd. Hoewel de parlementaire behandeling nog loopt, is het voor bibliotheken en cultuurorganisaties verstandig om nu alvast inzicht te krijgen in de mogelijke gevolgen. Extra kosten bij langdurig verzuim Langdurig verzuim brengt al aanzienlijke kosten met zich mee. Denk aan twee jaar loondoorbetaling, re-integratietrajecten, arbodienstverlening en vervanging van medewerkers. Als de compensatieregeling verdwijnt, komen daar mogelijk ook de kosten van de transitievergoeding volledig bij. De financiële impact kan aanzienlijk zijn. Een medewerker met twintig dienstjaren en een bruto maandsalaris van € 3.500 heeft bijvoorbeeld recht op een transitievergoeding van ruim € 23.000. Zonder compensatie zijn deze kosten volledig voor rekening van de werkgever. Daarmee wordt langdurig verzuim niet alleen een HR-vraagstuk, maar ook een belangrijk onderwerp voor directie, management, begroting en risicomanagement. Aandacht voor slapende dienstverbanden Ook de discussie rondom slapende dienstverbanden kan opnieuw relevanter worden. De compensatieregeling werd destijds ingevoerd om te voorkomen dat werkgevers dienstverbanden na twee jaar ziekte lieten doorlopen om betaling van de transitievergoeding te vermijden. items.title: De tanden in een meerjarenplan

items.title: 5 inzichten en 10 tips van het Nationale Bibliotheek Congres 2026
items.raw_text: Een recordaantal bibliotheekprofessionals, één gedeelde ambitie: bouwen aan een bibliotheek die voor iedereen van betekenis is. items.title: Maatschappelijk rendement: van kosten naar waarde
items.raw_text: Een taalcursus, digitaal spreekuur of leesbevorderingsprogramma kost tijd, geld en capaciteit. Maar wat levert zo’n investering eigenlijk op? Niet alleen voor de deelnemers, maar voor de samenleving als geheel? Bibliotheken en andere maatschappelijke organisaties maken iedere dag impact. Mensen worden taalvaardiger, digitaal zelfredzamer en doen actiever mee in de samenleving. Toch is die maatschappelijke waarde niet altijd zichtbaar in cijfers. Steeds meer organisaties zoeken daarom naar manieren om verder te kijken dan financiële resultaten alleen. Hoe maak je maatschappelijke impact inzichtelijk? En hoe laat je zien wat jouw inzet echt oplevert? In dit artikel ontdek je hoe je kosten en impact met elkaar verbindt en beter inzicht krijgt in de waarde van jouw organisatie. Wat is maatschappelijk rendement? Maatschappelijk rendement gaat over de verhouding tussen wat je investeert en wat je daarmee oplevert voor de samenleving. Het draait niet alleen om geld, maar ook om de maatschappelijke waarde die ontstaat door activiteiten en programma’s. Denk bijvoorbeeld aan een taalprogramma dat mensen helpt om beter te lezen en schrijven. Of aan een cursus digitale vaardigheden waardoor inwoners zelfstandiger worden. De effecten daarvan zie je niet direct terug op de balans, maar ze maken wel degelijk verschil voor mensen en voor de samenleving. items.title: ‘Veranderen doe je via consensus én met fermheid’
items.raw_text: Binnen Digitaal Doordacht onderzoeken we hoe digitalisering in de publieke sector daadwerkelijk bijdraagt aan betere dienstverlening, meer openheid en groter vertrouwen. Het veranderverhaal van Jolein Baidenmann laat zien dat echte openheid niet draait om simpelweg méér informatie openbaar maken, maar om informatie die voor mensen daadwerkelijk begrijpelijk en bruikbaar is. Wat haar aanpak bijzonder maakt, is hoe zij in een complexe publieke omgeving beweging creëert: door belangen zichtbaar te maken, partijen te verbinden en draagvlak te combineren met duidelijke keuzes. “Soms moet je als leider keuzes maken en stevig zijn: ik heb iedereen gehoord, maar we gaan toch die kant op.” Jolein Baidenmann is verandermanager en werkt met die insteek aan een overheid die openheid op een betekenisvolle manier probeert waar te maken. “Het is belangrijk dat een open overheid de samenleving in staat stelt om mee te denken, te controleren en gebruik te maken van de informatie die bij de overheid beschikbaar is.” Als manager Open Overheid en plaatsvervangend directeur Open Overheid bij het ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken en Koninkrijksrelaties (BZK) is Baidenmann bij uitstek de persoon om het concept ‘open overheid’ in praktijk te brengen. Sommigen bepleiten ‘radicale openbaarheid’, wat simpelweg neerkomt op álles openbaar maken. items.title: Vijf tips voor een (nog) betere samenwerking tussen bestuurder en CISO

items.title: Juli
items.raw_text: Online radicalisering van jongeren: het gesprek gaat door Deze maand is er opnieuw veel aandacht voor schadelijke en gewelddadige online netwerken. De NOS berichtte op 23 juli over de aanhouding van een jonge man die wordt verdacht van deelname aan een sadistisch Com-netwerk ofwel community. Binnen dergelijke besloten online groepen kunnen kwetsbare jongeren worden geronseld en aangezet tot zelfbeschadiging, misbruik en geweld. De actuele berichtgeving raakt direct aan de onderwerpen die op 22 juni centraal stonden tijdens het symposium Online radicalisering van jongeren: herkennen, begrijpen en handelen, georganiseerd door de ATKM, de NCTV en ECP. Onder leiding van dagvoorzitter Liesbeth Rasker gingen professionals, onderzoekers en ervaringsdeskundigen in gesprek over de vraag hoe online radicalisering tijdig kan worden herkend, zonder jongeren te snel te veroordelen of te stigmatiseren. Radicalisering begint vaak niet met een uitgesproken ideologie of een duidelijke intentie om geweld te gebruiken. Het kan beginnen bij menselijke vragen: wie ben ik, waar hoor ik bij en wie neemt mij serieus? Online groepen kunnen daarop inspelen en grenzen tussen humor, provocatie, uitsluiting en geweld geleidelijk laten vervagen. De rode draad in het symposium, de podcast en de actuele berichtgeving is daarom dezelfde: blijf nieuwsgierig, investeer in kennis van de online leefwereld en voer het gesprek voordat standpunten en gedrag verder verharden. items.title: Zomerblog Marjolijn Bonthuis
items.raw_text: “Worden we een museum?” Een persoonlijke zomerse beschouwing over Europa, AI en de stap van dialoog naar daadkracht Deze zomer lees ik Grand Hotel Europa van Ilja Leonard Pfeijffer. Het hotel in de roman staat symbool voor Europa: prachtig, rijk aan verhalen, maar vooral gericht op het verleden. Europa bewaart zijn kunst, architectuur en geschiedenis — en verkoopt die aan toeristen. Ondertussen wordt de toekomst elders gebouwd. Die gedachte dringt zich ook op wanneer ik kijk naar de huidige technologische ontwikkelingen. Terwijl Amerikaanse en Chinese bedrijven miljarden investeren in kunstmatige intelligentie, chips en digitale infrastructuur, zijn wij in Europa vaak vooral bezig met regels, risico’s en bescherming. Laat ik daar duidelijk over zijn: die aandacht is nodig. Zeker vanuit mijn dagelijkse verantwoordelijkheid voor digitale veiligheid, weerbaarheid en vertrouwen weet ik hoe belangrijk het is dat technologie niet zonder grenzen wordt ontwikkeld en toegepast. Big Tech heeft inmiddels zoveel economische, technologische en maatschappelijke macht opgebouwd dat stevige publieke kaders onvermijdelijk zijn. Bescherming van grondrechten, democratische controle en eerlijke concurrentie zijn geen luxe. Maar regels alleen maken ons nog geen speler. Als Europa vooral vastlegt onder welke voorwaarden technologie van anderen hier mag worden gebruikt, terwijl we zelf onvoldoende investeren in de ontwikkeling ervan, blijft onze invloed beperkt. items.title: Stichting ECP wijzigt structuur governance om ook in de toekomst bijdrage te kunnen leveren aan de digitale samenleving
items.raw_text: Om waarde te kunnen blijven toevoegen aan de digitale samenleving heeft Stichting ECP haar governance structuur aangepast. Eerder meldde Stichting ECP al dat ze de aanpassing aan het eind van dit jaar wil hebben ingericht, als uitkomst van een traject dat in 2024 in gang is gezet. Stichting ECP is er van overtuigd met deze governance structuur ook in de toekomst haar bijdrage te kunnen leveren via haar activiteiten en in samenwerking met het brede netwerk van publieke en private partijen die zich hiervoor inzetten. Stichting ECP wordt per 1 januari 2027 een zelfstandig opererende organisatie, die zelfstandig activiteiten uitvoert en beheert en worden activiteiten van de verschillende PPS-programma’s en -projecten opnieuw aanbesteed. Een overzicht van wijzigingen governance en inrichting Stichting ECP is aan het einde van dit bericht opgenomen. Met de voorgenomen aanpassingen in de governance structuur zal Stichting ECP uiterlijk 1 januari 2027 voldoen aan de Code Goed Openbaar Bestuur, inclusief de bijbehorende bevoegdheden, besluitvormingsstructuur, benoemingsprocedures- en termijnen en bezoldiging conform WNT, vertaald in de Statuten en het Bestuursreglement. In aanloop naar deze situatie is per 1 juli 2026 de huidige inrichting van de samenwerking tussen Stichting ECP en LunaVia B.V. beëindigd. items.title: IFLA Europe Regional Division Webinar 2026: How EURDC supports Libraries across Europe
items.raw_text: The IFLA Europe Regional Division invites library professionals, information specialists, and IFLA members from across Europe to an engaging online webinar on 1 October 2026 at 11:00 CEST . Over the past five years, the Europe Regional Division Committee (EURDC) has worked to strengthen collaboration, advocacy, and engagement among libraries and library professionals throughout Europe. Despite these efforts, many colleagues remain unfamiliar with the division’s mandate, activities, and opportunities for involvement. This webinar aims to change that. During the session, four members of the current EURDC Committee, representing Finland, Germany, Norway, and Portugal, will introduce the division’s work and share practical examples of how EURDC supports the European library community. Participants will gain insights into the division’s objectives, ongoing initiatives, and future priorities. The webinar will also provide an opportunity for dialogue. Attendees will be encouraged to share their expectations, discuss challenges facing libraries in Europe, and suggest ways in which EURDC can better support their work and professional communities. The event will be conducted in English via Zoom, with automated subtitles available to improve accessibility. Across these activities, common priorities emerged: strategic renewal, member engagement, leadership, partnerships, advocacy, financial sustainability, visibility, digital transformation and AI, resilience, crisis preparedness, and responsiveness to changing societal needs. These priorities are closely aligned with MLAS’s mission to support strong, well-managed library associations through leadership, peer learning, resource development, and effective association practices worldwide. items.title: The Great IFLA100 Futures Challenge
items.raw_text: Join us on the first stage of our drive to engage the global library field in a reflection on the future(s) of our institutions, our place in society, and our international cooperation. A key pillar of the programme for IFLA’s centenary year – IFLA100 – is a focus on the future. Alongside the remembering and celebration of our past achievements and the people that made them possible, we want this year to be a chance to build up the skills, attitudes and connections necessary to enter into our second century with confidence. Central to this is our work to build up the habit of futures thinking across our profession. This enables us to steer a path between a denialism driven by passivity, and an excessive reliance on specific predictions that leaves little room to react to the unexpected. IFLA already has a strong record of work in this space. Our Trend Report in 2024 shared a set of potential trends, as well as using these to offer a range of potential scenarios for the future, ready to be used by libraries and library workers to test their own plans. Our Weak Signals report added to this, using ideas gathered at the 2025 World Library and Information Congress to identify phenomena that could potentially have a transformative effect in the future. items.title: Call for Proposals: Consultancy on International Association Membership, Volunteer and Congress Models
items.raw_text: IFLA is looking for a consultant that can support work to ensure that our membership, volunteer and Congress financial models are optimised as we enter our second century, drawing on insights and best practice from peer organisations. This work takes place as part of our Sustainable Futures Journey, which brings together a range of initiatives intended to strengthen our Federation’s ability to deliver on its current and future strategies. The work on reviews of our membership, volunteer and congress financial models is being led by members of our Governing Board, with a strong emphasis on engaging our communities and partners, and drawing on their experience and ideas. At the same time, we are realistic about the fact that there are many other international associations which face similar situations to our own, and which can offer us valuable lessons and ideas to inform our own work. This is where we are seeking a consultant who can support the work of our Board by bringing together key examples and inputs. Details of our expectations are set out in the formal call , which is open until 15 September. We welcome applications from around the world, and from teams of consultants.

items.raw_text: IFLA Journal is pleased to announce a Special Issue on Public Libraries, Migration, and Inclusion: Comparative Perspectives and Emerging Practices. Rationale and Scope Public libraries worldwide are increasingly positioned as key institutions supporting the inclusion of people with migrant backgrounds, including immigrants and refugees. They provide access not only to information and cultural resources, but also to language learning, social participation, and civic inclusion. In doing so, libraries contribute to broader societal goals related to equitable access to information, inclusion, and democratic participation. At the same time, these roles are shaped by diverse national and local contexts, policy frameworks, and professional practices. Despite a growing body of research on library services for people with migrant backgrounds, comparative and cross-national empirical studies based on shared methodologies remain relatively limited. Much of the existing literature focuses on single-country case studies or localized initiatives, making it more difficult to identify broader patterns, structural differences, and common challenges across contexts. This special issue seeks to address these gaps by inviting contributions that explore the role of public libraries in relation to migration and inclusion from a range of international perspectives. items.title: Limiting Risk in the Face of Uncertainty
items.raw_text: If you save for retirement when you are young, the standard advice is to emphasize stock-based exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or mutual funds. Stocks increase and decrease in dramatic ways that no one can predict reliably, so this approach carries some risk. Fortunately for US stock market investors, that risk has historically been rewarded, on average and over the long term, with high returns. As you approach retirement and need to rely on investments to cover living expenses, the standard advice is to shift your portfolio toward bond-based ETFs or mutual funds. Bonds have had fewer and less dramatic booms and busts. For this reason, they are generally considered less risky than stocks. On average, over the long term, bonds’ safety has meant lower, more reliable returns than stocks. Risk makes less sense for ALA right now. Because of its financial deficit , the Association needs stability. Therefore, in April, ALA’s Endowment Trustees updated the target allocation for the Association’s investment portfolio, reducing our holdings of stocks from 50% to 40%, and increasing ALA’s holdings of bonds from 30% to 40%. As a result, we are sacrificing some projected returns to limit projected risk. If stocks boom as they have in the past few years, ALA’s portfolio will not increase as much as it would have. items.title: Secrets of Effective Upskilling
items.raw_text: This is an excerpt from Upskilling for Library Workers: A Guide for Future-Ready Professionals by Ann Medaille (ALA Editions, 2026). With the advent of new technologies and rapid social and economic shifts, library workers’ jobs are being transformed. Compared with a decade ago, library workers now spend more time consulting on complex research tools, teaching digital literacy classes, supporting virtual learning environments, helping users troubleshoot devices, and codesigning projects with community partners. The pace at which library staffers are called upon to learn new skills is accelerating, and workers may struggle to keep up. In addition, automation and artificial intelligence (AI) are altering many aspects of work. In the long run, technological innovations have the potential to increase productivity and lead to more interesting kinds of work, but in the short term, they often cause disruptions that can be difficult for workers to navigate. To address these changes—and manage the anxieties that come along with them—workers need constant support for skill development. While corporations may embrace upskilling to stay competitive, libraries will have to support upskilling to remain relevant. Library leaders are under greater pressure to respond rapidly to changing social and economic conditions and demonstrate that their libraries make a difference in their communities. items.title: Hold the Phone
items.raw_text: Since fall 2024, each school day at Grant High School in Portland, Oregon, has started the same way: Roughly 2,100 students line up to place their phones in gray and green Yondr pouches—the kind live performers use to prevent audience members from recording—as they enter the building. From the morning bell to dismissal, phones are sealed and can be unlocked only with special magnets near the school’s exits as students leave for the day. The high school’s effort to limit phone use on campus has received support from its educators, who say classroom engagement is on the rise, and mixed reviews from students, who dislike being cut off from their devices. But there’s been one unexpected outcome of the policy: More students are spending time in the library, where they’re browsing the collection or hanging out during free periods, says teacher-librarian Paige Battle. “They’re checking out more books, and I feel like that’s been so important in their education,” Battle says. “We’re seeing studies about students, even adults, not having the reading stamina they’ve had in the past, so I’ve been encouraged by this increase.” Roughly six in 10 parents of an 11- or 12-year-old say their child owns a smartphone, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey . And as more schools across the country enact phone-free policies—29 states and the District of Columbia have instituted bell-to-bell phone-free policies so far—many school libraries are experiencing a surge in popularity. items.title: Mall Wonder
items.raw_text: After serving its community for nearly 45 years in the same building, Escondido (Calif.) Public Library closed in April 2025 for an $11.6 million renovation. It was important to us, as the city’s lone library, to preserve access during construction. So one month later, our library opened a temporary location in a very different kind of facility: the nearby North County Mall, where services and collections were spread across six storefronts, including a former Abercrombie & Fitch clothing store. Of course, moving a library takes more than a month. Our planning took more than a year and required staff to work under tight deadlines, limited budgets, and high expectations. Here’s how we did it, and what we learned from the process. Choosing a location. It’s essential to consider whether the new location will match, improve upon, or limit access. Retailers and mall operators have already studied traffic patterns, visibility, parking, and nearby amenities. Leverage that knowledge to evaluate access. In our case, the public benefited from a highway and bus stop near the mall, and adjacency to a city park. The arrangement also gave the mall a stable civic tenant and created natural cross-traffic between library patrons and shoppers. The mall was not just available space; it was a location where public access, economic development, and community visibility could overlap. items.title: Dismantling Disinformation
items.raw_text: Library workers are well aware of the effects of book bans and censorship. Propaganda and disinformation are the flipside of the same coin. Understanding the complex relationships among these interrelated processes is more critical than ever, especially as libraries explore possible solutions and responses. The following books show how disinformation can lead to censorship and how censorship can, in turn, allow disinformation to thrive. Book Bans, Disinformation, and Cultural Erasure: The Censor­ship Movement in Libraries, Schools, and Society By Paul T. Jaeger Jaeger situates the current book-banning movement within a larger social and political effort to erase marginalized communities and culture. He provides clear definitions and examples of these processes and goals, including the roles played by technological progress and economic inequity. With accessible references (like the Beatles, Dungeons & Dragons, and Holmes and Watson) and nuanced examinations of McCarthyism, the history of libraries, and the myth of neutrality, this is a recommended read for anyone interested in a more expansive understanding of current First Amendment challenges. items.title: A Sense of Purpose
items.raw_text: When it comes to building resilient and equitable communities, libraries are natural leaders. We provide places where neighbors meet, learn, and support one another; where sustainability education becomes action; and where residents can find year-round climate refuge. When communities are resilient, they are better able to overcome barriers. The Obama Presidential Center (OPC) branch of Chicago Public Library (CPL) is an example of a library that strengthens the social infrastructure that underpins resilience. CPL Commissioner Chris Brown describes the branch as a civic platform for residents, artists, educators, and organizations to cocreate the life of the library and its surrounding public spaces. Though just 5,000 square feet, OPC was designed to spark connection, invite conversation, and inspire activities that encourage ­socialization and enjoyment. The branch partners with such nonprofits as the Art Institute of Chicago, the literary arts group StoryStudio Chicago , and the artist-led alt_Chicago . OPC is a striking example of how libraries do not just serve resilient communities, they help create them. On the Gulf Coast, sustainability is a daily requirement. Lindsay Cronk, dean of Tulane University Libraries in New Orleans, has shared that the library’s partnership with Keep Louisiana Beautiful , a state program, helps connect students, faculty, and staff with opportunities for conservation, beautification, recycling, and environmental action. items.title: Association of American Publishers (AAP) and The Authors Guild Release New Study Analyzing the Impact of Library E-Lending on Commercial Book Markets
items.raw_text: From a Joint Release: Today, the Association of American Publishers (AAP) and the Authors Guild announced the release of a landmark independent study by leading economists at Secretariat Advisors, titled An Empirical Study of the Impact of Library E-Lending on the Book Economy. The study, commissioned jointly by AAP and the Authors Guild, but independently conducted by Secretariat Advisors’ economists, provides the most rigorous analysis to date of how the steep shift toward digital lending in recent years has affected the commercial marketplace for books in the United States, specifically, the consumer sales on which authors and publishers rely for financial success. The research concludes that increased digital access to e-books through library apps influences consumer behavior and impacts commercial markets across both physical and digital formats. The study further concludes there is robust and economically meaningful evidence of direct substitution between library e-lending and retail sales and that decreases in library e-book prices or certain other changes to licensing terms, as required in recent state legislative initiatives, would cause further harm to commercial markets. items.title: Report: Arkansas Librarian Fired After Opposing Book Ban Efforts to Receive $275K in Settlement
items.raw_text: From the Arkansas Advocate: A central Arkansas county agreed this week to pay $275,000 to the former library director who was fired after speaking against local conservatives’ push to limit children’s access to books. Saline County announced Thursday it had reached a settlement with Patty Hector, who had been the county library’s executive director when she was fired in October 2023. County Judge Matt Brumley’s firing power came from an ordinance approved by the all-Republican quorum court, which previously urged Hector to move books with “sexual content or imagery” out of children’s reach. Hector alleged in her 2025 legal complaint that her firing was retaliatory and violated her First Amendment right to free speech. The case was set to go to trial next week before Monday’s settlement hearing. U.S. District Judge James Moody signed off on the settlement Wednesday. Hector said she hoped the settlement would send a message to librarians and other public servants that their constitutional rights matter. Two respected collaborators will join HathiTrust in this effort: Northeastern University Library, which brings deep expertise in digital scholarship, and Authors Alliance, a nonprofit that supports authors who want their work to benefit the public. With a firm commitment to lawful, noncommercial, public-interest uses, this project will make HathiTrust’s 19 million digitized volumes more useful and accessible to the academic community and the public. Transparent Books: AI Infrastructure for Discovery and the Public Interest responds to the growing need for shared, trusted, academy-led infrastructure enabling sophisticated discovery and research of digitized collections. The project aims to connect readers to relevant titles more efficiently, thereby enhancing their reach and impact, and will consider a range of interests, including publishers, authors, scholars, and members of the public. items.title: Art for Everyone: How Public Libraries Expand Access
items.raw_text: Introducing children to viewing, creating, and enjoying art at a young age helps them appreciate it throughout their lives. Some children are exposed to various forms of art because it is part of their daily life or because they have easy access to museums and galleries in their community. But in many areas across the country, access to museums and art galleries can be cost prohibitive. That is where the public library comes in! While some museums, including the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., offer free admission, millions of people across the country do not have easy access to them. According to the 2024 Annual Survey of Museum-Goers from the American Alliance of Museums and Wilkening Consulting, museum admission costs vary widely, from a few dollars to $40–$50 per adult at some institutions. Among U.S. adults who visit museums at least occasionally, cost was the number one barrier to visiting more often. Among frequent museum-goers, younger adults were twice as likely as seniors to be concerned about admission costs. In response to those barriers, and in an effort to enrich and inspire customers of all ages, many library systems have stepped up to provide access to art in a variety of forms. Borrowing Art from the Library Brooklyn Public Library in New York recently launched a lending program featuring art by local artists. items.title: “I Want You To Stay Up Late To Finish The Book” — Juno Dawson On Her Chilling “Survival Show”
items.raw_text: Juno Dawson’s Survival Show begins with an irresistible premise: a reality TV show where contestants vie for one of five spots in a band, where each week the lowest-ranking contestant gets executed on live television. Dawson centers the book around Taryn Beck, a gutsy seventeen-year-old who’s survived a climate disaster and war and now lives in a refugee camp with her father and critically ill brother. When Taryn lands a chance to audition for Starmaker , the television show that has become a global phenomenon and launched past winners to superstardom, it seems like the best opportunity for her to provide her brother with desperately needed medical care. Yet when she begins rehearsing with her fellow contestants, Taryn must confront the challenge of collaborating and competing with contestants whose success could mean her death. Intrigue and romance quickly follow, and Dawson balances the gloom of her dystopian setting with a dark wit. Dawson previous books include This Book Is Gay and Clean, and critics have heaped similar praise on Survival Show . In their starred reviews, Publishers Weekly wrote, “This chilling, satirical dystopian adventure defies expectations,” and Kirkus stated, “Fast-paced and heart-wrenchingly suspenseful, this work combines the glitter, drama, and cutthroat competition of the pop music industry with the looming threat of death.” Author photo courtesy of Eivind Hansen. items.title: Autism Acceptance at All Ages
items.raw_text: Autism acceptance efforts have come a long way in recent years, and libraries are one of the key reasons why. As a librarian and the mother of two sons with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), I’ve witnessed this progress firsthand. In my capacity as the assistant director of the Beals Memorial Library (BML), I’ve seen how efforts to create more inclusive programs, services, and spaces can promote positive social change that dra-matically improves people’s quality of life, disabled or not. Through our “See Beyond the Spectrum” initiative, in recent years, BML has established new ASD-friendly programs, made our existing programs more accessible, updated our collections with texts by autistic writers, and established an autism caregiver support group. Our staff have gone through autism awareness training, and we’ve established partnerships with local organizations that serve autistic youth. Much of this workhas been supported by external grants, including generous funding from the ALA’s “Libraries Transforming Communities” initiative, which seeks to help libraries become more accessible to patrons with disabilities. Everything we’ve done has proved beneficial, both inside and outside of the library. Staff-patron interactions are more productive and less awkward. Families feel welcomed, and patrons with ASD feel comfortable being themselves when they visit. Community members are more knowledgeable about ASD and are actively talking about it. items.title: The Librarian’s New Role: Knowledge Discovery
items.raw_text: For more than thirty years I have been interested in one deceptively simple question: How do we find things? At first glance, the answer appears obvious. We search. But anyone who has spent a lifetime in libraries knows that searching and finding are not the same thing. Throughout my earlier articles in Public Libraries Online , I explored several aspects of this process. In Finding Answers , I argued that patrons rarely come looking for information; they come looking for answers. In Search vs. Research , I suggested that locating information is only the beginning of inquiry. In Keeping Things Found , I examined what happens after discovery, how knowledge is preserved, organized, and made retrievable for future use. Artificial intelligence is now transforming how people search and, perhaps more importantly, how they find. For the first time in history, millions of people no longer begin by opening a directory, consulting an index, or scanning pages of search results. Instead, they ask a question in ordinary language and receive what appears to be a finished answer. This is more than another improvement in search technology. It represents a fundamental change in the relationship between people and information. The question librarians should be asking is not whether artificial intelligence can answer questions. items.title: How Library Science Principles Power Community AI Literacy
items.raw_text: Public libraries are dealing with budget cuts, book bans, and the usual existential questions about whether anyone needs physical collections when they can google everything. And now AI shows up, and everyone assumes libraries are about to get steamrolled by it too. But watch what’s happening at reference desks across the country. Patrons ask how to determine whether an IRS email is real or a phishing attempt generated by AI. Small business owners are trying to figure out which AI tool won’t steal their marketing copy. Retired community members want to use AI to parse dense municipal documents but do not know where to start. A parent is concerned about their teenager using AI for homework and whether that’s cheating. These aren’t edge cases. This is what reference work looks like now. Much has been written about how libraries can use AI tools internally—chatbots for reference, algorithms for cataloging, and predictive analytics for collection development. But there’s another question we need to answer: How do libraries help communities navigate AI? And here’s what I realized while building AI governance frameworks: these are not computer science problems. They’re library science problems—questions about provenance, access, evaluation, and trust. The exact questions libraries have been answering for over a century, just dressed up in a new syntax. items.title: Tag! You’re It: RFID’s Big Play in Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology has become one of the most influential innovations shaping the future of library operations. Since its introduction into library settings in the late 1990s, RFID has steadily evolved from an experimental enhancement to a widely adopted tool for improving circulation, inventory management, and patron experience. As libraries continue to modernize and adapt to changing user expectations, understanding RFID, including its capabilities, limitations, and long-term implications, is essential for informed decision-making. This article provides a thorough overview of RFID technology in libraries, synthesizing research, case studies, and industry standards to help public librarians evaluate whether RFID is the right investment for their institutions. Understanding RFID Technology in Libraries RFID tags come in two primary forms: active and passive. Libraries exclusively use passive tags, which do not require an internal power source and are small enough to be concealed within books and media cases. Passive tags contain information that is picked up by a scanner, while active tags emit their own signals. In library settings, RFID tags store essential item information like title, author, call number, and location and can be read without direct line-of-sight. items.title: Making the Invisible Visible: Advocacy at the Heart of Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Public libraries face no shortage of challenges today. Ongoing censorship efforts, increasing threats to staff safety, growing public distrust of institutions, and rapid technological change continue to reshape the work of libraries and the people who sustain them. In this environment, advocacy matters more than ever. That message came through clearly at the 2026 Public Library Association conference, where many sessions focused on helping librarians strengthen their advocacy skills. At the heart of every library are the workers who understand its value best and are often its strongest advocates. One session I attended, “Advocacy at the Core of ALA’s Next 150 Years,” featured Sam Helmick, Maria McCauley, Daniel Montgomery, and Lisa Varga. The panel offered practical strategies for advocacy, including using easy digital tools to contact legislators, participating in National Library Legislative Day, supporting legislation such as the Right to Read Act, and inviting elected officials into library spaces to see the work firsthand. Another standout session, “Advocacy Strategies for Getting Things Done,” featured Lisa Wells, Amanda Kordeliski, Tim Miller, Gail Oehler, and Kelly Sitzman from libraries across Oklahoma. Their discussion focused on the power of quiet advocacy. Quiet advocacy means building relationships with legislators before you urgently need their support. items.title: Creating Meaningful Connections Through Memory Cafés
items.raw_text: The 2026 Public Library Association conference featured many excellent sessions focused on programming and community engagement, but one that especially resonated with me was “Memory Cafés in Libraries: Creating Meaningful Connections,” presented by Christina M. Johnson, Allan M. Kleiman, and Susan H. McFadden. Before attending this session, I had heard of Memory Cafés but did not fully understand what they were, who they served, or how they could be integrated into library programming. By the end of the hour, I felt equipped with the knowledge and resources needed to successfully bring this type of program to my own library. The library where I work is within walking distance of two senior living apartment buildings, and our community of 16,000 is also home to several assisted living facilities. Older adults often make up the majority of attendees at our programs, so as the staff member responsible for adult programming, I attended PLA hoping to learn about meaningful services for this audience. The session began by defining the core audience for a Memory Café: people living with dementia, whether formally diagnosed or not, their caregivers, and volunteers interested in learning more. The presenters emphasized the importance of clearly communicating this audience in promotional materials. Christina M. items.title: From Skeptic to Troublemaker: One Book Club Idea That Changed My Mind
items.raw_text: I’ll admit it: library book clubs make me instantly wary. People constantly ask libraries to offer them, only to never actually show up. And a book club for kids? Forget about it. They already have plenty of assigned reading at school. So when I attended Tanvi Rastogi’s session, “Speak Up: Using Middle Grade Books to Build Allyship Muscles,” I assumed it would be a low-stakes hour to slowly wake up and drink my coffee. Friends, I didn’t even need the coffee. I left energized. Rastogi’s book club model, Good Books Young Troublemakers (GBYT), is far more than a well-intentioned idea with a catchy title. It has its own website and 501(c)(3) tax-exempt status, a sign of just how thoroughly Rastogi developed this concept after first dreaming it up in the shower. She has created a turnkey model for anyone interested in starting a chapter. Each month features a thoughtfully selected recently published title, paired with a robust downloadable discussion guide. New chapter leaders can request a starter kit complete with stickers and bookmarks mailed directly to them. Best of all, it’s free, though donations are encouraged, and there’s a pretty fun sticker if you decide to support the work. So what is GBYT all about? items.title: Renewed and Reenergized: A Rural Librarian’s PLA 2026 Experience
items.raw_text: It was a true gift to attend the recent Public Library Association Conference in Minneapolis. It had been 12 years since I last attended PLA, and I had forgotten just how exciting and energizing it can be to gather with library workers from across the country. I returned home reinvigorated, renewed, and more excited than ever to be part of our increasingly important community of librarians and information professionals. The morning keynote sessions featuring Bryan Stevenson and Dr. Ruha Benjamin were especially galvanizing. Stevenson shared how his grandmother changed his life by nurturing his love of reading, opening doors that a young boy from Alabama could scarcely have imagined. I am still reflecting on Dr. Benjamin’s perspective on AI, which she reframed, in part, as Ancestral Intelligence rather than Artificial Intelligence. The closing session with Lakota chef Sean Sherman felt especially meaningful as my library prepares to host the Americans traveling exhibit. Each of these “big idea” sessions broadened my perspective, helping me look beyond the borders of my small rural community and glimpse the larger conversations shaping our profession. The welcoming remarks from PLA President Brandy McNeil were timely and encouraging, and I was grateful to meet her and express my appreciation in person for the scholarship that made my attendance possible. items.title: Finding Connection and Community at PLA 2026
items.raw_text: Attending the PLA 2026 Conference in Minneapolis was an enriching experience in my professional development as a second-year MLIS student. I first learned about PLA while working as a Library Assistant and later as a Library Associate at my local public library system in Maryland. At the conference, I attended sessions on a range of topics, connected with library professionals, and shared time with fellow members of APALA. Having taken MLIS courses focused on children’s literature, multicultural resources, and the future of libraries, I was especially eager to learn more about early literacy services. In the session Intentional Early Literacy Outreach to Hispanohablantes , Andy and Carina from Arapahoe Libraries shared best practices and lessons from their efforts to connect with Spanish-speaking families. Although I am not a Spanish speaker, I appreciated the Spanish live captions throughout the presentation. One of the most valuable aspects of the session was the presenters’ candid discussion of what did not work. For example, they found that holding community meetings indoors at an apartment complex limited resident participation. Their experience highlighted the importance of time, persistence, and relationship-building with community management. They also shared a practical communications lesson: changing the language on promotional flyers to lectura gratuita , with emphasis on gratis , helped clarify that the sessions were free. items.title: “I Wanted To Write Something That Felt More Like A Hug” – DeAndra Davis On Her Enchanting Coming-Of-Age Novel
items.raw_text: Despite being smart, funny, and her class’s valedictorian, Jaliya has spent much of her high school career ignored by her classmates. After graduation, her dad encourages her to leave their South Florida home to spend the summer in Jamaica with her family, who she hasn’t seen in several years. Although reluctant to do so, Jaliya changes her mind after receiving an unsigned letter postmarked from Jamaica asking when she’s going to return there. Convinced the letter is from her estranged mother, Jaliya devises a plan to return to Jamaica, find her mother, and figure out once and for all why she left their family long ago. Yet once she’s back in Jamaica, Jaliya’s life grows unexpectedly richer. She reconnects with childhood friends and finds herself caught in a love triangle between her schoolgirl crush, Andre, and an intriguing new girl, India, who has just moved to her cousin’s neighborhood. DeAndra Davis’s The Lovers, The Liars, And Me is a tender coming-of-age story that sensitively handles estrangement, coming out, cultural identity, and the complicated feelings that arise when you enter the adult world. In its starred review, Booklist raved “this lyrically written novel is centered around nuanced and deeply lovable characters, and Jaliya is a protagonist who readers will want to grow and change with as she figures out her own path.” Davis spoke with us about crafting complicated relationships, allowing her teen characters to make mistakes, and capturing the first-generatio

items.title: Expanding Access Through Inclusive Collections
items.raw_text: Receiving a scholarship to attend PLA 2026 in Minneapolis gave me the opportunity to learn from innovative libraries and inspiring information professionals. One session in particular, “Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities,” presented by Plano Public Library and Libraries for All LLC, reinforced a simple but urgent idea: if members of our community cannot meaningfully use our materials, we are not fully meeting our mission. Access is about more than having a collection. It is about ensuring that everyone can engage with and benefit from it. The session highlighted how people with disabilities are often underserved by traditional library collections. While many libraries offer large print, braille, and other accessible formats, these resources do not address the full range of patron needs. Some readers may have physical disabilities that make turning pages difficult. Others may benefit from visual supports, tactile elements, or alternative ways of interacting with a text. Without intentional efforts to address these needs, some community members may remain excluded from library services. Before attending the session, my understanding of accessibility largely centered on traditional formats such as large print and braille. Learning about adaptive books expanded that perspective. items.title: Connections, Ideas, and a Little Hope: Reflections from PLA 2026
items.raw_text: I had the distinct honor of attending PLA 2026 in Minneapolis thanks to a PLA scholarship. As an eastern North Dakota native, Minneapolis is a familiar destination, but spending several days surrounded by thousands of energized library professionals made the city feel vibrant and new, despite the wind, cold, snow, and more wind. The connections, reunions, and conversations I experienced throughout the conference reminded me why gatherings like PLA matter. Alongside reconnecting with colleagues and making new professional connections, I left with fresh ideas, practical tools, and renewed optimism about the future of libraries. Several sessions stood out to me, both because of their content and because of the presenters who brought those ideas to life. One of the first sessions I attended was “Becoming One Library: How to Build Better Internal Communications,” presented by Mary Kapusta of Calgary Public Library. Kapusta was engaging, funny, honest, and refreshingly candid about both the successes and challenges of implementing a completely redesigned internal communications strategy across 23 library branches. What impressed me most was how scalable the ideas felt. Calgary Public Library serves nearly 1,000 employees, while my library employs roughly 30 staff members, yet many of the concepts felt immediately applicable. Instead, I left with a notebook full of starred ideas, half-written thoughts, and questions scribbled in the margins. Looking back, those messy notes reveal the sessions that stayed with me long after the conference ended. Conversations about internal communication, programming for older adults, and flexible, community-centered services challenged my assumptions and sparked new ideas for my own work. Sessions including “Becoming One Library: How to Build Better Internal Communications,” “Aging Together: Library Programming for Older Adults,” and “Memory Cafes in Libraries: Creating Meaningful Connections” reframed how I think about serving both staff and patrons. items.title: Building More Inclusive Libraries for Patrons with Disabilities
items.raw_text: At every conference I attend, I hope to leave with at least one idea I can realistically adapt and implement at my own library. At PLA 2026, I found that inspiration in my very first session: *”Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities.”* Presenter Courtney Walker, founder of Libraries for All, shared how her experience as a school librarian led her to rethink traditional picture book collections for students with disabilities. She noticed that many students were not engaging with standard picture books, often returning them unread or damaged. In some cases, families stopped checking out books altogether. Seeking a solution, Walker adapted a resource commonly used in classrooms: laminated books enhanced with sensory and interactive elements. By modifying these materials for library use and creating durable books with touch-and-feel components, she found that students with disabilities engaged more actively with stories and enjoyed more positive and equitable reading experiences. Walker now works as a consultant through Libraries for All and collaborated with fellow presenters Janet Cox and Maggie Fox of Plano Public Library (PPL) in Texas to develop a full collection of adapted books. Their team selected popular picture books, organized volunteer workshops to create adapted versions, trained staff to support the collection, and developed cataloging practices for these unique materials. items.title: Information Strategies for Libraries in the Age of AI
items.raw_text: Librarians must actively adapt to an information landscape increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence (AI), search engine optimization (SEO), and algorithm-driven content. During the PLA 2026 session, *”Trust & Verify: Information Accuracy in the Age of SEO, AI, and Algorithms,”* Nathaniel Burnard, Systems Services Manager at Allen County Public Library, offered a practical and timely examination of how these forces influence the way we, and our patrons, discover and evaluate information. As a 2026 PLA scholarship recipient, I had the opportunity to attend Burnard’s insightful presentation in Minneapolis. Burnard began by explaining the differences between misinformation, disinformation, and malinformation (MDM). While these terms are often used interchangeably, they differ based on the intent behind the creation or sharing of information. Misinformation is false or inaccurate information shared without intent to deceive. Disinformation is deliberately false information created to manipulate, mislead, or cause harm. Malinformation contains truthful information that is presented in a misleading, sensationalized, or harmful way. To help identify MDM, Burnard encouraged attendees to ask critical questions such as, “Does this content provoke a strong emotional response?” and “Does it use small pieces of valid information that have been exaggerated or distorted?” He also emphasized the importance of avoiding engagement with misleading content. items.title: One Year Later: The Digital Equity Act Cancellation and Libraries
items.raw_text: May 8, 2026, marked the one-year anniversary of the Trump Administration’s cancellation of the Digital Equity Act (DEA). The $2.75 billion Digital Equity Act was a part of a coordinated effort to provide communities across the U.S. with high-speed broadband and the skills and technology needed to thrive in our increasingly digital world. Libraries and other community anchor institutions were integral to the planning of this once-in-a-generation opportunity to address the digital divide. Collectively, these groups spent precious resources and staff time applying for DEA program grants, leading related coalition building efforts, and conducting outreach and asset mapping. The abrupt cancellation of the DEA grants last year was a significant blow to digital inclusion programs nationwide, impacting millions of Americans. According to the Idaho Commission for Libraries , over 80% of the state’s DEA Capacity Grant award “was slated for subgrants supporting rural Idahoans, including older adults and veterans.” Public and tribal libraries across the state would have benefited from grants to replace outdated computers to offer public training on cybersecurity and technology use. In Maine, nearly 130,000 people would have been directly served by DEA-funded programs, such as digital skills training, technical support, telehealth access, and affordable device programs. items.title: Rennie McDougall On How Social And Historical Forces Molded Twentieth Century Dance
items.raw_text: Rennie McDougall ‘s Nonstop Bodies: How Dance Shaped New York City gives readers a thrilling new perspective on twentieth century New York City by investigating the different choreographers, dancers, and dance movements that flourished there during that time. McDougall guides the reader through various dance movements, from the marathon dances of the Prohibition era to the Lindy Hop to the Rockettes and beyond. All the while, he catalogues the dense web of lineages that developed among specific dances and artists, allowing readers to see relationships among disparate dance forms that might not be immediately apparent. McDougall also dives into how social and historical forces directly molded the evolving dance forms, and the unique position New York City held to create countless connections between dancers and choreographers not only in the moment, but across time as well. Critics have heaped praise on the book, with Library Journal hailing it as “a love song to dance in all its forms and the city that invented and perfected so many styles.” McDougall spoke with us about taking a different approach to dance history, bringing readers into the immediacy of dancing, and how the texture of the dancers’ lives unconsciously affected the evolution of dance. items.title: Leading Public Library Groups Call for E-book Action
items.raw_text: ULC, PLA, CULC/CBUC, COSLA, ARSL, seek sustainable pricing for digital access for all readers As community demand continues to ramp up, organizations representing the vast majority of North American public libraries today released a joint statement calling for change in licensing for digital content. The explosion in usage is straining public library budgets and dragging down wait lists for readers in ways that are not sustainable. While libraries are able to purchase physical books and lend them indefinitely, digital content is typically licensed to libraries for a limited time, check-out limit, or both. And, while consumers pay $13 for an e-book on average, libraries typically spend magnitudes more for a two-year license, often $55 or more. “Publishers, authors, and public libraries should be partners, but with the exponential growth in digital content demand, libraries are unable to provide and sustain access under current licensing models. The moment is ripe for large publishers to meet with libraries across North America, to hear our concerns, and address them, so we can continue building a mutually beneficial future for literacy and reading.” — Brooks Rainwater, President and CEO, Urban Libraries Council (ULC) “America’s public libraries are critical to digital discovery of authors and titles, as well as literacy builders and champions. items.title: Learning Across Generations at PLA 2026
items.raw_text: AI, Teen Workforce Development, and Culinary Literacy in Public Libraries Attending PLA 2026 provided valuable opportunities to explore new ideas for programming, community engagement, and lifelong learning in public libraries. As the director of a small rural library, I especially appreciated sessions that offered practical strategies that could be adapted for smaller communities with limited resources. One session that stood out to me focused on AI-powered book clubs and digital literacy programming for older adults. The presenters shared how a small public library developed a program that combined traditional book discussions with hands-on experiences using generative AI tools. Participants used AI to explore book themes, ask questions, and connect stories to current events and broader issues. What I found especially valuable was the way the program used technology to encourage discussions about banned books, intellectual freedom, misinformation, and media literacy, while also helping older adults build confidence using new tools in a welcoming and supportive environment. The session provided practical ideas for creating similar programs, including facilitation strategies, technology recommendations, and activities that connect literature, technology, and community learning. It reinforced how libraries can support lifelong learning while reducing barriers to technology use for older adults. Another memorable session was Teens Lead Internship: Building a Sustainable Future

items.title: Trust, Verification, and the Role of Libraries in the Age of AI
items.raw_text: Librarians must actively adapt to an information landscape increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence, search engine optimization (SEO), and algorithm-driven content. During the PLA 2026 session Trust & Verify: Information Accuracy in the Age of SEO, AI, and Algorithms , Nathaniel Burnard, Systems Services Manager at Allen County Public Library, offered a practical and timely examination of how these forces affect the way both librarians and patrons locate and evaluate information. As a PLA 2026 scholarship recipient, I had the opportunity to attend Burnard’s presentation in person in Minneapolis. Burnard began by explaining the distinctions between misinformation, disinformation, and malinformation (MDM). While these terms are often used interchangeably, the intent behind the information matters. Misinformation refers to false or inaccurate information shared without intent to deceive. Disinformation is deliberately false information intended to manipulate or cause harm. Malinformation involves true information presented in misleading or sensationalized ways that may still cause harm. Burnard encouraged attendees to ask critical questions when evaluating information, including: Does this provoke an emotional reaction? Does it use small pieces of valid information that have been exaggerated or distorted? items.title: Reflections on Accessibility, Teen Services, and Lifelong Learning
items.raw_text: With only a few hundred words to reflect on my first PLA experience, it was difficult to decide which sessions and ideas I wanted to highlight. I took something away from every presentation I attended, but perhaps the most compelling idea came from Bryan Stevenson’s keynote address: “Our strength as a democracy is rooted in willingness to learn.” I firmly believe there are always ways we can improve ourselves and our work, which is exactly why I wanted to attend PLA. Public librarianship is constantly evolving, and no library is perfect. I wanted to learn how other libraries are adapting services and programs to better meet the needs of their communities. One session that immediately stood out to me was Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities. I was so inspired by the presentation that I emailed my manager halfway through the session to discuss how we could begin implementing adapted books into our collection right away. Presenter Courtney Walker shared how she recognized a need within her own community and developed adapted books that provide equitable access to the same stories and materials, rather than offering entirely separate alternatives. Walker emphasized that adapted books do not alter the stories themselves. No words or images are removed, and no pages are omitted.
